articles.body: A CSV import can show an unexpected character before the first header name even when the visible text looks right. Check the file's opening bytes before changing the header or resaving the export. This read-only program reports whether the file begins with the three-byte UTF-8 signature. 1. Make the practice files A byte is a small unit of stored data. UTF-8 is an encoding that turns text characters into bytes. Some programs put the bytes EF BB BF before the text as a signature, often called a byte order mark or BOM. UTF-8 does not need a byte-order choice, so the name does not mean these bytes control the order of the rest of the file. Save this as MakeExamples.py in a practice folder: from pathlib import Path Path ( " Plain.csv " ).

articles.title: I Built an Offline AI Agent That Answers Business Questions With File-and-Line Proof
articles.excerpt: Last quarter I asked a general-purpose AI chatbot: "Which product should I restock first?" I pointed it at three CSV exports — sales, inventory, and customer feedback. It answered confidently: SKU-A,…
articles.body: Last quarter I asked a general-purpose AI chatbot: "Which product should I restock first?" I pointed it at three CSV exports — sales, inventory, and customer feedback. It answered confidently: SKU-A , because "it appears to be selling well." SKU-A was fine. The real problem was SKU-C : selling 100 units a week with only 6.3 days of stock left against a 14-day supplier lead time. In ten days that SKU is out of stock, and every week of outage costs roughly 100 units of revenue. The chatbot couldn't see that, because it never actually joined the files — it skimmed the column names and guessed. That failure is what DecisionLens is built to prevent. What DecisionLens does DecisionLens is an offline, zero-dependency decision agent written in pure Python standard library.

articles.title: SOLID
articles.excerpt: I'm not talking about a state or matter but a set of five design principles for object-oriented programming: Single Responsibility Open/Closed Liskov Substitution Interface Segregation Dependency Inve…
articles.body: I'm not talking about a state or matter but a set of five design principles for object-oriented programming: Single Responsibility Open/Closed Liskov Substitution Interface Segregation Dependency Inversion. Introduced by Robert C. Martin, they describe how classes and modules should be structured so that code stays maintainable, extensible, and testable as it grows. Each principle addresses a different aspect of class design — how much a class should do, how it should handle change, how sub-types should behave, how interfaces should be shaped, and how dependencies between modules should be organized. Together they form a general vocabulary for describing what "good" object-oriented design looks like, and why certain structures tend to hold up better than others over time.

articles.body: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon.
